lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Cost of Choosing
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi (V2) | Lesson 1 -- The Cost of Choosing
lesson.grammar_point: present habits: state vs action verbs and frequency language

paras: You made your first decision of the day before you were properly awake: get up now, or in nine more minutes. By tonight you will have made thousands more. Most of them are mundane. What to eat. Which message to answer first. Whether the paint on the wall is close enough to the colour you had in mind. Not one of them is hard. Together, they are exhausting.

Psychologists call this decision fatigue, and the idea is simple enough to be uncomfortable: every choice, however small, spends a little of the same limited supply. Deciding is work, even when the stakes are trivial. And when the supply runs low we do not stop deciding. We simply decide worse. We default to whatever is nearest. We postpone. We say yes, because saying no would take an argument we no longer have in us.

The evidence is ordinary enough to recognise. Shoppers at the end of a long day reach for whatever is nearest to hand, and spend more money doing it. Judges reviewing case after case grant fewer favourable decisions as the morning wears on, and recover after a break. Some people wear more or less the same clothes every working day, not out of indifference, but to remove one more question from a day already full of them.

What follows is not a lecture about willpower, and this is the part people get wrong. Willpower is not the muscle being worn down here. Attention is. So the useful advice is structural rather than moral. Settle the trivial questions once, and stop asking them every morning. Keep the decisions that matter for the hours when you are still fresh. Cut the number of options before you start weighing them up, because weighing up is where the cost sits.
There is a trade-off, of course. A life with fewer decisions in it is a life with slightly less of you in it. So the question was never how to decide less. It is which decisions are worth the tank.

gist.prompt: Which sentence comes closest to the argument of the whole text?
choices: People who make bad decisions in the evening are people with weak willpower.
Every decision costs a little attention, so the fix is to have fewer of them, not to try harder.
Shopping and court decisions are the two areas where tiredness matters most.
The best way to decide well is to compare as many options as possible.

items: The writer says that tiredness makes people stop making decisions.
The text says: 'when the supply runs low we do not stop deciding. We simply decide worse.'
According to the text, small decisions and big decisions draw on the same supply.
The text says: 'every choice, however small, spends a little of the same limited supply.'
The judges in the example became more favourable as the morning went on.
The text says they 'grant fewer favourable decisions as the morning wears on, and recover after a break.'
The writer thinks the problem is a lack of willpower.
The text says: 'Willpower is not the muscle being worn down here. Attention is.'
The writer accepts that removing decisions has a price.
The text says: 'There is a trade-off, of course. A life with fewer decisions in it is a life with slightly less of you in it.'

infer.title: Not written down. Work it out from the text.
items: The writer says the idea is 'simple enough to be uncomfortable'. Uncomfortable for whom, and why?
Why does the writer call the advice 'structural rather than moral'? What would the moral version sound like?
The last line asks which decisions are 'worth the tank'. What is the tank, and what does the metaphor suggest about it?
The writer never says the word tired about the judges. How do we know that is the explanation?

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gist = b. The argument is structural, not moral: fewer decisions, not more effort.
True/False = F, T, F, F, T.
Rhetorical function: thesis / example / recommendation / example / recommendation.
Gap-fill: mundane, worn down, weighing up, default to, trade-off.
State verbs take no -ing: know, seem, prefer, matter. Action verbs do: weigh up, compare, postpone, decide.
